A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is proposed, relying solely on the data from a depth camera without the need for any specialized equipment or setup procedures. The proposed method utilizes a robot to create various poses, acquiring depth images and corresponding joint positions through forward kinematics. The depth data is then processed using a point-based registration algorithm to estimate the robot's pose, with a fully autonomous cycle taking approximately 6 seconds in simulation. The method's performance is comparable to traditional methods when using markers, with an average error of 3.5 millimeters for pose estimation and 5 degrees for orientation in simulation.

A new model is introduced that combines the K-Nearest-Neighbors (KNN) interference structure with treatment variability. Within this framework, the receipt of a treatment by unit i affects the outcomes of units j, with j=i or j's outcome changing, with positive probability less than 1/2. Building on the KNN model, an efficient test is developed to determine treatment interference in a given unit, i. Under the null hypothesis that treatment has no effect on i's outcomes, to be compared with a normal distribution having a mean of zero, an asymptotically normal distribution is derived for the test statistic under specific conditions. Simulation results indicate that the proposed test performs well even under small sample sizes and that its results don't differ significantly from those obtained using ideal conditions.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within neutron stars have shown significant emissions at distances from the star's surface, potentially detectable through neutrino bursts from supernovae or within newly formed neutron stars. These emissions are primarily driven by a mediator particle that facilitates dark matter particle interactions, with a choice of mediator particle type impacting neutrino emission levels. In a new study, researchers examined the neutrino emissions resulting from annihilation of dark matter particles using a pseudoscalar mediator, finding higher neutrino emission rates at greater distances from the star's surface in this scenario compared to emissions mediated by a gauge boson. They also discovered that surface layers of neutron stars could be directly probed by dark matter particle detectors, potentially leading to new insights into dark matter physics, and that the observed neutrino emissions could significantly exceed expected emissions from core nuclear reactions, reaching levels of tens to thousands of s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$
  s deg$^{-1}$ deg$^{-2}$.

The ongoing UNIONS project, a photometric survey with the Fourth Data Release, has enabled researchers to study the large-scale structure at cosmic distances and weak gravitational lensing effects with high precision. To analyze these effects, we employed ShapePipe, an open-source pipeline that utilizes machine learning and neural networks to accurately measure galaxy ellipticity and position, ultimately contributing to the UNIONS four-band catalog. In this research, we outline the steps and validation of ShapePipe, and then apply the measurements to map the weak gravitational lensing signal across approximately 400 square degrees of the UNIONS footprint at a 5 sigma confidence level. We observed a significant signal aligned with the direction of cosmic massive structures, and the amplitude of the shear signal matches that expected from the cosmological principle at a 2 sigma confidence level.

Building upon the work of Kronecker and Weyl, notable results were established by Jager and Peluse, revealing the exact degree of exactness in the exactness of a specific orbit over a prime set, which in turn connected to a long-standing issue in diophantine approximation. In this research, we expand upon Jager and Peluse's findings, taking a broader approach by removing the prime restriction and replacing it with a logarithmic criterion. Additionally, we revisit the original diophantine issue, breaking down its complexity and substituting it with a more manageable challenge. Notably, our new hypotheses hold significant potential in resolving the original problem of Salem and Spencer.

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its lab-created origin, the material is prone to significant thermal fluctuations at relevant experimental temperatures. Using nuclear magnetic resonance, we were able to measure the magnetic dynamics within the material and quantify the strength of these correlations. Based on our findings, we developed a theoretical framework combining mean-field theory with BKTP characteristics to describe this behavior. The results showed that the correlations in [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2 are comparable to those seen in more robust, structured magnets like Nb. Importantly, we were able to determine that an applied magnetic field can either intensify these correlations or eliminate them entirely, depending on their strength and orientation. This unique sensitivity to external magnetic fields makes [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2 an exceptional material for studying magnetic phenomena and conducting precise, experimental research into quantum magnetism.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact dark matter composition, and as a result, sterile neutrinos dominate the dark matter population. The $a\nu$MSM model is compared to both direct and indirect dark matter detection methods, with the result that the model accommodates neutrinoless double beta decay at the Weizsacker-Williams scale without conflict. The analysis concludes by highlighting the need for a more comprehensive understanding of dark matter, as well as double beta decay, in order to effectively test sterile neutrinos within this framework.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can precisely represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$, surpassing the previous best-known estimate of $\alpha\leq 0.463$. This advancement leads to a reduced classical simulation time of quantum circuits containing $N$ qubits and executing $T^m$ operations, from $O(3^m \cdot 2\log^m N)$ to $O(2^{\alpha m} \cdot 2\log^m N)$.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
corresponding to the complex quintessence field and its complex conjugate, 
within the framework of FRW universes. We derive equations of state, 
effective equations of state, and expansion histories for each scenario, 
focusing on the real part's implications. We find that both scenarios 
predict an accelerating universe, with differences arising from 
the effective equations of state and phase transition redshift values.

Between August and October 2020, the LAMOST began operating its $K$2 plates, which enable the observation of up to six targets in the optical spectrum for up to six 30-minute visits each night. Due to their moderate spectral signal-to-noise ratios, these objects cannot be classified using traditional methods. Our study employed a combination of spectral features and machine learning to identify and analyze the spectral characteristics of 94 unique targets that were visited at least six times and exhibited variability. We present spectral feature measurements for 88 stars and confirm the existence of 94 targets, which include 4189 spectral measurements. To establish a baseline for further research, we have released these data through the Vizier database. By identifying and tracking these variables, we can gain insights into their behavior and characteristics.

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. Existing implementations have relied on adjusting the supply voltage to maximize bit uncertainty within a desired operating range. However, these approaches required manual calculation to determine the optimal voltage for maximum uncertainty. This optimal voltage was typically not achieved due to limitations in accurate entropy extraction. To address this issue, this study proposes the TuRaN SRAM-based TRNG, which can automatically determine the SRAM array's operating voltage for maximum bit uncertainty. Furthermore, TuRaN incorporates a novel error correction scheme, reducing the impact of reading errors on output bits and enhancing overall output quality. Experimental results demonstrate that TuRaN outperforms comparable designs, validating its efficiency and effectiveness.

A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been developed, incorporating two linear molecules that interact electrostatically: one molecule is a single-electron transistor and the other is a single-electron trap. To confirm our design's validity, a theoretical analysis was performed, integrating ab-initio electronic structure calculations with a general single-electron tunneling theory. The outcomes demonstrate that these molecular constructs can operate as resistive switches, including a set of devices that function as logical NOT gates and a memory array, all functioning at room temperature.

We introduce a comprehensive approach for computing complex, multi-dimensional integrals based on sophisticated mathematical relationships between loops and numbers. This methodology is utilized to break down complex mathematical objects called Feynman integrals into simpler expressions, which can be numerically evaluated. We outline a step-by-step strategy for representing and analyzing the Feynman integrals, and provide a detailed case study for a specific integral relevant to particle physics. This study involves a complex calculation at the three-loop level for a scenario with four particles interacting. The numerical evaluation of the integral is performed while maintaining precision, and the results are compared with calculations using different techniques to verify consistency.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to a comparable result for one-dimensional continuous-time Markov processes. A related statement concerning the invertibility of a specific transition matrix is also demonstrated.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations and quark fraction, the model reveals a significant range in which hybrid stars are comprised entirely of quarks, and estimates a maximum mass of around 3.2 solar masses.

The $q$-deformed optomechanical system, which deviates from conventional physics with a specific value of $q$, has been studied to see how it affects the behavior of light when it interacts with a moving mirror. By using the properties of $q$-deformed bosonic operators, we were able to develop a study on the system's eigenmode and eigenfrequencies. Our research also included the study of light's electric field, which helped us observe the amplification of light as well as the transparency and enhancement of optical output when certain conditions are met. Furthermore, by applying the $q$-deformation, we were able to enhance the effects of these phenomena.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited all necessary properties of negative parity states. Building on this work, I explored the R-parity conservation aspect in a model consisting of right and left rotors by imposing a specific condition on their orientations. As a result, I derived a set of wavefunctions for the 2+ and 2- states, and calculated their respective masses and transition strengths between these states and 0+ states. Notably, I found that the transition strengths displayed a significant gap at an energy level roughly in the middle of the gap between the 2+ and 2- states, consistent with experimental observations in even-even nuclei.

We investigate the spin and orbital fluctuations in model ultrathin Haase-Slichter transition metal dichromium films using a quantum cluster version of the dynamic mean-field theory, taking into account the complex interplay between electrons. The effects of spin-orbit coupling and an in-plane anisotropy due to the substrate on the film's spin and orbital moments are considered. The films exhibit various types of orbital ordering, including a unique 120-degree phase, which is stabilized by a combination of spin-orbit coupling and an in-plane anisotropy. The spin and orbital moments in the films are flanked by significant orbital polarization, leading to a non-zero total orbital magnetic moment. The type and magnitude of this polarization depends on the effects of spin-orbit coupling and an in-plane anisotropy. The unique properties of the films could potentially be harnessed for the development of novel spin-orbit coupled devices.

This study examines the statistical behavior of laser-cooled atoms trapped in an optical lattice dissolving into a normal Bose-Einstein condensate. The investigation assumes a situation where net momentum transfer from lasers results in a systematic phase shift, ultimately leading to a BEC-like phase transition through a thermodynamic process. We analyzed the changes in number distribution, condensate fraction, and momentum using the Bogoliubov approximation, observing a significant departure from Gaussian number distribution as the BEC transition is approached. Additionally, our results for atom momentum reveal a power-law behavior with exponent dependent on the rate of dissipative processes occurring within the optical lattice.

This study delves into the cryptocurrency trading network's structure, examining both short and long-term connections among cryptocurrencies. To capture complex relationships among multiple assets, we employed a degree-based correlation network to analyze the relationships among cryptocurrencies. For weekly time frames, our findings reveal a cluster structure dominated by USDT and high-performing cryptocurrencies such as ETH and BTC. However, this cluster dissipates in daily time frames, which are instead characterized by a dominant group of major cryptocurrencies. Our results also suggest that trading volumes significantly influence the network's structure, particularly in daily frames. Furthermore, our research reveals that extreme volatility often corresponds to changes in the network's structure, revealing a dynamic and evolving relationship between cryptocurrency prices and trading activity.

The formation of particles from atmospheric pollutants is a crucial process influenced by chemical and physical reactions involving sulfuric acid and water. The role of vibrational motion in particle formation is a topic of ongoing debate, with computational tools available to investigate this role. This study employs the path-integral method to calculate the properties of small sulfuric acid and water clusters, comparing their behavior with corresponding classical ensembles. The results indicate that, at present temperatures, vibrational effects are relatively minor, but may become more significant at warmer atmospheric temperatures. However, the study does suggest that an improved theoretical approach is necessary to accurately describe the behavior of sulfuric acid monomers.

We establish the definitions for a compact perception pair, compactified perception space, and compactified perception, along with developing concrete methods to construct these structures. Our work culminates in the creation of a compactified space of group equivariant non-expansive operators, with a specific example being the compactified perception space of a Euclidean space.

The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity's effect in space. In studying this, we investigate whether there's a universal connection between temperature gradients and flow velocities across all types of materials. We examine this through two main perspectives: one that relates to the material's internal energy and another that considers the flow of entropy. By looking at both cases, we analyze a specific type of thermal flow and find that it doesn't follow the expected gravitational analogy or entropy relation as seen in entropy conductive materials. As a result, we see unusual behaviors such as negative thermal resistance and sound waves with negative group velocities.

In various situations, simpler models tend to outperform their complex counterparts, but the underlying mechanism often remains unclear. For neural networks, improved generalization over complex models might be attributed to regularization techniques, such as dropout or batch normalization, although their direct effect has not been extensively demonstrated. By reinterpreting dropout and batch normalization in terms of perturbation and feature selection, we show that many neural network architectures, enhanced with these components, tend to prefer simpler models. The evidence supporting this claim comes from experiments in both fixed-weight and during training scenarios.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice.

Automated essay grading is a difficult task due to the vast possibilities of student writing.
Despite this challenge, numerous approaches have been proposed over the years.
In recent times, deep learning models have gained prominence in AEG due to their ability to learn complex patterns in data.
Both transformer-based models and traditional recurrent neural networks have been effectively employed in solving this problem.
In addition to using labeled data for training, transfer learning, and ensemble methods to improve performance, advanced techniques such as ensemble learning can also be utilized to overcome the limitations of small dataset availability in achieving good results.
This study explores the effect of data augmentation using pre-trained language models BERT and RoBERTa on transforming raw student essays into numerical scores.
By applying these techniques to transformer models, including BERT, RoBERTa, and BART, significant improvements in performance were achieved, with evaluation accuracy exceeding 94% and external validation yielding 0.083 and 0.070 in mean absolute error (MAE) in the AIPSE and PASE datasets, respectively.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals arising from such marginal independence models, with a specific focus on models for random graphs and matroids' independent set polytopes. We also explore numerical methods for parameter estimation through both Euclidean distance and maximum likelihood techniques and establish a database for small model examples.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize the overall value of these opportunities, they should be reserved for individuals who are further away from benefiting from them. Additionally, the greatest societal gain often arises from providing opportunities to those who are closest to achieving them. Through analysis of a simple model, the overall impact of these allocations becomes maximized when opportunities are distributed equally across different groups in society.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of signcryption components from both the sender and receiver, as well as a one-time signature from the receiver using a public key.
However, in the Delegated RingCT model, validators serve as public keys for receive requests, necessitating modifications to signcryption and one-time signatures to accommodate forged receive requests from malicious delegates.
Furthermore, Delegated RingCT must resist delegate impersonation attacks, making existing signatures vulnerable.
Our solution leverages tweaked one-time signatures that are resistant to impersonation attacks from delegated public keys found in Delegated RingCT.
By incorporating Delegated RingCT in dash, we have fixed critical issues, including delegate impersonation, forged receive requests, and transaction tampering, as evidenced by recent attacks on the network.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within the same space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have observed the production of W boson pairs in association with a Z boson in proton-proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy level. This observation was made using a dataset with a total luminosity of 137 inverse femtobarns, gathered by the CMS experiment at the LHC. Two events involving the decay of these bosons into notable particle groups, specifically either electrons, muons, or tau particles, and either pairs of opposite charge muons or pairs of opposite charge electrons, were analyzed. Statistical modeling indicated that the production of these events occurred at a rate that matched 5.5 sigma beyond when assuming a production rate of 6.9 nanobarns, representing a three-standard-deviation excess over expected background levels. Furthermore, theoretical models based on two different approaches, an approach considering quantum corrections in the strong interaction and an approach considering the electroweak interaction, suggested a total production rate of these events to be around 6.9 nanobarns for WZ production when considering the decay of these bosons into electrons, muons, or tau particles. Two events involving the decay of these bosons into pairs of opposite charge muons were analyzed. Statistical modeling indicated that the production of these events occurred at a rate that matched 4.7 sigma beyond when assuming a production rate of 6.9 nanobarns, representing a two-standard-deviation excess over expected background levels. Furthermore, theoretical models suggested a total production

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, found primarily on the web. This research paper addresses this issue by introducing a new, open-access UD Hebrew treebank, created using an advanced, highly-accurate annotation system. This innovative approach leverages machine learning to efficiently produce high-quality annotations for large datasets in just a few hours. The new Hebrew treebank consists of 13,000 sentences, which have enabled training state-of-the-art, domain-agnostic models that surpass earlier efforts. When evaluated on the new corpus, these models perform significantly better than before, achieving impressive results, with 47 F-score points higher than the previous best attempts.

We establish that for any $1 \le p < \infty$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists an $\varepsilon$-isometric map $\Phi: \ell_p \to \ell_p$ with the property that for any subset $A \subset \ell_p$, the dimension of the image of $\Phi(A)$ under the canonical embedding is less than or equal to $(1+\varepsilon) \dim A$. Our result enhances a previous finding by Alaei, Krahlik, and Mendel with reduced dimensionality constant and extends it to $\ell_p$ for $1 < p < \infty$.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the development of data-driven modeling in engineering and science. This surge is largely attributed to extensive research efforts and the increasing availability of high-quality data. However, individual institutions face challenges in making a significant impact due to limited resources and data accessibility. To overcome these obstacles, institutions can collaborate, combining their expertise and knowledge to create more effective data-driven models. This concept is known as cooperative data-driven modeling. By sharing data and analytical capabilities, co-operating partners can leverage their combined potential, paving the way for substantial advancements in the field.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose a novel framework for constructing degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, which can be applied to various binary channel models. Our framework also allows the creation of LDPC ensembles with degree-degree correlations that exhibit superior error-rate performance compared to their fully uniform counterparts.

An advanced module system consists of interconnected modules with predictable behaviors, enabling the analysis of complex systems by treating safety issues at the module level. However, ensuring each module is safe when connected to other modules is a significant challenge. We've developed a method, called the Safety Filter, to verify if a given module can be safely integrated into another module without disrupting its safety characteristics. The Safety Filter employs a System-Level Synthesis approach, analyzing the modules' dynamics and control interactions to determine if safe coordination is possible. If such coordination exists, the Safety Filter identifies all safe control strategies for the modules, whereas if not, it pinpoints the obstacles to safe coordination. We've successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of the Safety Filter through a simple driving scenario.

A critical flaw exists in the current quantum key distribution (QKD) system, which could be exploited by malicious hackers. To address this vulnerability, the experts introduced a new, improved protocol designed to enhance the security of QKD. Employing random phase randomization when generating the states used in QKD has been suggested as a potential solution. However, if the randomization process is incomplete - affecting only some of the states while leaving others unchanged - it could be manipulated by hackers to breach the system. We identify the specific conditions under which this improved protocol remains insecure and propose possible remedies to fix the issue.

Recent research has shown that large, finely-tuned language models can pick up words to complete sentences, a capability known as in-context learning. Our study explores whether such models can also learn from smaller, more diverse training datasets, even when those datasets are not part of their initial training. We examined four different training strategies, each using a varying amount of data from different sources (WikiText, BookCorpus, WebText, and a custom dataset) in varying orders (either all at once or in a sequential build-up). We discovered that when training on a sequence of datasets, a significant improvement in performance is observed, but only when each new dataset is significantly smaller than the previous one. When training on datasets of a similar size or larger all at once leads to better results. Interestingly, the order in which datasets are presented also has an impact, particularly when training from the smallest to the largest results in better performance overall, a finding particularly true when training on the web-based dataset WebText.

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, but little is known about what happens when the initial, intricate structure of these formations disintegrates. To investigate this process, we conducted a series of simulations combining magnetic fields, radiative cooling, and thermal conduction, which revealed that the formation of kiloparsec-scale, filamentary structures is a common outcome when the initial cooling complex breaks apart. The presence of magnetic fields significantly influences the length and thickness of these filaments, while changes in thermal conduction affect the formation of a central hub within the cluster's core. The rate at which material cools and forms stars is not diminished by these structures; in fact, our simulations indicate a slight increase in star formation efficiency.

The investigation of CP violation in beauty and charm decays serves as a crucial test of the Standard Model's precision and also serves as a vital indicator for potential deviations from the model. The measurement of CP violation processes in these areas relies heavily on accurate analysis of data from experiments, particularly in decays that are sensitive to the weak phase, known as $\Delta\beta$. This phase can be determined by examining ratios of observables derived from decays involving hadronic or semileptonic modes, known as the $\Delta\beta$ ratio. Recent findings from experiments have revealed CP violation in numerous areas, including direct detection, semileptonic decays, and $B^0$ decaying into a combination of charged pions and electron-positron pairs. This review will delve into the current state of CP violation research, with a focus on the latest measured values and, when applicable, comparisons with predictions made by the Standard Model and other theoretical frameworks.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have unique polarization properties and their counterparts in bosonic string theory are significantly weaker. A remarkable relationship exists among these amplitudes, where one is proportional to the others. A previously proposed theory, known as the Gross conjecture, suggests that this proportionality holds for all string interactions. Although the conjecture's validity has been confirmed for previously calculated amplitudes, its scope remains uncertain for other interaction types. To address this question, the newly discovered amplitudes are analyzed, and their consistency with the conjecture is verified. Additionally, the string scattering matrix is found to be singular at a specific energy threshold, a characteristic consistent with the conjecture's predictions.

This paper proposes a set of network management procedures that enable and guarantee the operation of multiple service types over a shared cellular network. Specifically, we develop closed-form formulas and optimization techniques for managing a cellular network with limited resources, using demand information obtained through pricing mechanisms. We apply these management procedures to ensure sufficient service capacity for demand patterns that may fluctuate seasonally or randomly. We also ensure sustainable resource usage by preemptively allocating resources to certain services during peak periods, thus preventing resource starvation for other services. Furthermore, we address the complex issue of coexistence between multiple network technologies, and present simple, efficient strategies for managing a shared pool of resources by different technologies.

This study explores the feasibility of zero-resource speech synthesis without transcription, instead using basic acoustic units as input, which are identified through unsupervised end-points detection algorithms. We compare the quality of speech synthesis in a zero-resource setting, specifically in Arabic and Korean, using two approaches: transforming units in isolation, and re-synthesizing units while sequentially combining them over time. While the quality of the isolated units appears higher than that of the time-sequential representation, we observe that the improvement decreases as the size of the unit inventory increases. We also examine the impact of the size and quality of the unit inventory on speech synthesis in a zero-resource context, finding that speech generated with a large, high-quality vocabulary sounds more natural and resembles reference speech more closely.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging combinatorial optimization issue, requiring intricate data processing. To tackle this problem, we introduce a novel multi-stage optimization framework, combining coupled convex programming with data-driven McCormick envelope relaxation, to enhance computational efficiency. By leveraging data from previous solutions, we introduce new variables, constructs, and constraints within each planning stage to optimize the robot's movement. We implement our model on both a simulated two-joint planar force-couple optimizer and a six-limbs humanoid robot, achieving significant performance improvements.

We have developed a streamlined method for determining the minimum number of measurements and operations required to transform one quantum state into another, likely involving only basic measurements and simple operations like cloning, discarding, and mixing.
To illustrate the utility of our method, we have obtained precise estimates for the number of measurements and operations needed to achieve various multi-copy quantum compression goals.
Our method also enabled us to derive a precise upper limit for the number of measurements and operations needed to achieve full distinguishability in multi-copy settings.
Furthermore, our analysis led to the derivation of a precise lower limit for the number of operations required to achieve full convertibility in multi-copy settings, which coincides with a previously discovered limit in certain single-copy scenarios.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, causing the pendulum's resonance frequencies to shift. In the scenario of vertical excitation, the averaging method helped to establish resonance conditions, which were confirmed by numerical integrations. When both types of excitation were present, the averaging method led to a set of reduced differential equations. The phase trajectory of the averaged system was obtained through numerical integration, with results indicating that the averaging method accurately represented the motion of the coffee cup. This was further validated through numerical integrations of the original equations, both with and without accounting for energy dissipation.

In our research paper, we tackle the challenge of regularized distributionally robust learning in decentralized networks. By combining robustness to data variation with regularization, our method can effectively balance accuracy and model smoothness in diverse decentralized learning settings. We develop a reliable decentralized algorithm, DR-DSGD, to solve the regularization-based minimax problem. The algorithm's robustness is achieved through the use of an entropy function in the minimization term and a quantization function in the maximization term. We establish tightness of the chosen entropy and quantization functions for regularization, along with novel concentration inequalities for quantized random variables, which enable our analysis. The DR-DSGD algorithm's convergence rate is quantitatively characterized in terms of the network graph, quantization levels, and robustness parameter.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and final-stage entropy or particle multiplicities in relativistic nuclear collisions. By mapping energy onto a geometric plane, where radial and longitudinal sizes are represented by coordinates, we discover that entropy or multiplicity is directly proportional to initial energy, regardless of system size or collision type. This relationship holds for various centrainties and is consistent across different collision types, such as proton-proton, proton-lead, and lead-lead interactions. Furthermore, we find that particle yields and ratios, as well as entropy production, can be predicted solely based on experimental measurements of the energy state at a fixed stage and are unaffected by specific details of the initial condition and fluid dynamics.

Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, the process by which powerful jets form is studied under different magnetic field strengths and mass accumulation rates. The results show that strongly magnetized clouds produce fast-moving jets only when the protostar gains a relatively small amount of mass per year, typically no more than 10 to the minus 2 solar masses. However, this low-mass rate also means the protostar takes longer to form, typically more than 500,000 years. For clouds with weak magnetic fields, the protostar grows faster by around 10 solar masses per year, but in these cases, the fast-moving jets do not easily connect to slower-moving outflows. Instead, most of the material from these high-velocity jets gets wrapped around the protostar, eventually forming a jet nozzle that helps to establish a slower-moving outflow. The slower-moving outflow is powered by material that flows from the cloud, rather than the protostar's mass gain rate, and is capable of removing up to 10 times more material from the cloud each year.

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). A novel approach involves introducing a performance safety assessment (PSA) metric that measures system safety in the presence of overextensions, beyond performance boundaries. The PSA formula is adaptable to various balanced control filtered backstepping designs and can be optimized through different weighting parameters. By adjusting these parameters, the designer can balance performance and safety, yielding numerous optimal solutions. Each optimal solution corresponds to a specific set of BPC weighting parameters, which can be utilized in real-time to prevent overextensions, ensuring the system stays within its operational limits at all times.

This study provides estimates for the weak and exact resonances that occur between a planet and two nearby celestial bodies, and analyzes how these resonances affect an object's orbit under the influence of yardstick models. To establish these estimates, a method from Michtchenko and Roig's 2007 research is utilized, and its application is expanded to account for yardstick models. To validate the estimates, a numerical test is conducted that compares the results with actual mean-motion resonances studied by Ceccanese and Libralle in 2018.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. By comparing different approaches to representing the crystal electric field, we evaluate the accuracy of a new method against traditional approximations for describing excitons in two-dimensional materials. Our analysis shows that a specific approach, incorporating the velocity operator and correcting for discontinuities, preserves the symmetries of the electronic problem, even when coupled with an external electromagnetic field, a property it uniquely possesses. We demonstrate the impact of this symmetry preservation through the exact reproduction of exact eigenstates and eigenvalues across different light intensities. Furthermore, we find that this symmetry-preserving approach outperforms other methods in accurately modeling excitonic states across a range of light intensities.

This study addresses the crucial object recognition tasks of pose and shape estimation, which are now more feasible due to PASCAL challenges and widespread object categorization tasks. Despite significant progress in these areas, object recognition remains a complex task, particularly when instances vary in shape. To achieve optimal results, this research proposes an ideal recognition framework, taking into account only perfect object representations. Pessimism is the approach for dealing with imperfect data; therefore, a robust method based on reliable PASCAL category keypoints is developed for pose and shape estimation tasks. The proposed PASCAL keystone dataset of optimized 2D and 3D object models serves as a benchmark for evaluating category-level recognition performance. The newly introduced PASCAL dataset of 286 optimized 3D models demonstrates the potential for improved recognition results compared to traditional methods. The analysis reveals that PASCAL category-specific recognition excels at identifying object shapes but struggles with pose accuracy due to the limited availability of object orientation data.

We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By considering the Cauchy distribution's parameters as a single complex parameter, combining location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$ as $\gamma = \mu + i\sigma$, we will determine a region within the complex plane, ultimately defining it as both a disc and a square using a straightforward formula.

A new statistical method is developed to assess the sample size required for basket trials that involve multiple subgroups, allowing for information sharing between these groups. Typically, basket trials aim to find treatment benefits across various patient subgroups. Our method calculates the intended power for detecting a treatment effect within a specific subgroup while considering the potential benefits of borrowing strength from other subgroups. To achieve this, our approach employs a Bayesian framework that incorporates multiple testing and prioritizes subgroup-specific effects over overall treatment effects. As a result, the intended power for a given subgroup in a basket trial is equivalent to the power for detecting an effect within that subgroup in an isolated trial that borrows strength from other subgroups.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a balance of high-speed and high-accuracy capabilities. However, conventional control strategies often struggle to meet these requirements, particularly in motion systems that are susceptible to changes based on their position. This research introduces a innovative sequential loop closing control method that proactively detects and accounts for the expected variations in motion performance during the planning phase. Once an optimal trajectory is determined, the controller executes a refined motion follow-up process, utilizing real-time system data to make precise adjustments and minimize the impact of disturbances. This innovative approach allows for the design of motion systems that can maintain a high level of accuracy even in the presence of significant performance variations, effectively increasing the available working area. This methodology is then successfully applied to a real-world example, demonstrating its effectiveness and superiority over existing control methods.

We introduce a general, self-supervised method for partial-to-partial registration called PRNet, which can handle complex, irregular shapes and missing data. Conventional deep learning approaches for shape registration that rely on global features and global transformations may struggle with partial data and are often simplified or made brittle as a result. In contrast, our PRNet approach is robust and efficient, using only the information it needs to learn a compatible transformation for the input shapes. By employing a self-supervised point-to-point registration loss based on corresponding shape features, PRNet improves registration results, even with limited and missing data. Our method outperforms existing supervised methods in a variety of partial registration tasks and also achieves better results than the current best two-stage self-supervised approach. Additionally, PRNet reduces training time, eliminates the need to collect expensive paired shape datasets, and allows the method to be adapted to handle partial data by simply removing irrelevant data during training.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree by finding the least integer c such that the quotient $G/\gamma_{c+1}(G)$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property. For generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_n$, we derive the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of their nilpotent quotients $\Gamma_{n}/\gamma_{c+1}(\Gamma_n)$.

Instead of automatically assuming that unusual events at high-energy colliders signal new physics beyond the Standard Model, we should first verify the stability of the SM itself before exploring other possibilities. At low energies, this goal can be achieved through precision experiments, but at higher energies, it requires direct observation of the SM's electro-weak symmetry breaking process, specifically by searching for distinct signatures of the SM's Higgs boson's natural instability. We compare the sensitivity of various colliders, including future proton-proton, proton-electron, and heavy-ion colliders, as well as past and present B-meson facilities, to the critical parameter that indicates the SM's instability, $m_H^2/(m_H^2-m_f^2)$, with focus on observable phenomena that can be easily detected in experiments. Despite the limitations of some non-proton colliders, our analysis reveals that they might still contribute significantly to establishing the SM's instability, particularly if nature sets the mass of the unstable Higgs boson near a few GeV.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from experiments, which are often disrupted by uncertainties and incomplete signal extraction due to instrument limitations. This leads to inaccurate results, which can be corrected for using a technique refined in this study. This technique uses data from experiments over time to create a comprehensive map of how a system changes over time. This is done by accounting for uncertainties and using experimental readings to correct for biases in the findings, ultimately resulting in a reliable outcome. This technique is successfully tested and validated using data from NMR experiments.

We present the results of the first calculations of the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for several mesons, specifically $D^*$, $D^*_s$, $\rho$, $\phi$, $K^*$, and $J/\Psi$. This calculation also yields distribution amplitudes for the vector kaon, providing confirmation of lattice QCD predictions; in contrast to expectations, we find a nearly symmetric longitudinal distribution and an obliquely shaped transverse one, indicating a substantial contribution to momentum from the strange quark.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it is proven that short-time Fourier transforms within one-parameter spaces, ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, decay at a rate determined solely by $s$. Moreover, it is demonstrated that our results and smoothness criteria provide a characterization of Toeplitz operators on these spaces.

Segmentation of unseen image modalities poses significant challenges for deep learning models, as their training typically relies on well-annotated data from a single modality. To address this issue, we present a novel approach called Cyclic Segmentation GAN, which leverages a generative adversarial network to enable deep convolutional networks to segment images across different modalities without relying on ground truth data. By integrating cycle consistency and adversarial losses, our method allows the segmentation network to generate accurate semantic segmentations from both the source and target image modalities. As a result, the segmentation network is able to transfer its knowledge across different modalities through training, thereby achieving state-of-the-art performance on the MS-COCO dataset and surpassing several recent approaches on the CamVid dataset.

Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine
learning, including parameter sharing and radial basis functions, to anticipate
actions from visual scenes. It consists of an encoding module, a radial basis function
layer, and a recurrent neural network, all working in tandem. The encoding module
extracts distinctive features from an image, which are then fed into a radial basis function
layer. The output of this layer is subsequently processed by a recurrent neural network
trained to forecast future action sequences. Empirical evaluations have demonstrated that
our algorithm surpasses various competitors on JHMDB-21, UCF101-24, and UT-Interaction
datasets in terms of accuracy performance.

The 1985 great flare that occurred on April 12 against the cool star in the binary system AD Leo was thoroughly observed in detail. In the near ultraviolet spectrum (from 2200 to 3600 Angstroms), the emission behavior of the white dwarf was identified, contrasting with the disk spectrum. We used the observations of the IUE satellite to create a model of the emission spectrum of the flare. The thermal expansion of the outer atmosphere of the disk and the ionization of metals in the region produced the observed ultraviolet radiation. The time frames of IUE and UBV photometry revealed that the optical radiation originated from the thermalized outer layer of the expanding material, whereas metals were photoionized by the white dwarf's radiation. The photoionization of metals caused a red shift in the optical spectrum due to the inverse He I opacity effect.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the metric and the almost G2 structure on nearly G2-manifolds with this property.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on the space such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression, and a multi-variable operator $T$ can be defined as a composition operator with an arbitrary complex function $\psi$ for functions that are compatible with $\varphi$. This paper examines the conditions under which such an operator $T$ can be classified as C-normal for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, the study targets p-core p'-partitions which adhere to these constraints. Notably, the largest of these p-core p'-partitions are examined when p is a prime number greater than 3. The largest of these partitions can be predicted by simulating a random walk on a graph with a finite number of vertices. The outcome of this walk determining the largest partition when the number of p elements is very small. The probability distribution resulting from this walk is not the standard distribution for this type of graph since the largest partition is not equally likely to be the result of the random walk. The difference in probability distributions is most noticeable when very few p elements are included. When a single p element is included, the largest p-core p'-partitions are predicted to occur 27.8% of the time, as opposed to 11.76% for the standard distribution.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains such as vehicle navigation but have been shown to be vulnerable to manipulation with 3D mesh attacks, which can be generated using simple transformation-based techniques. Unlike image manipulation, 3D mesh manipulation has not been heavily researched, likely due to the complexities of modeling geometric data. To address this, we introduce a robust classification module for point cloud models called Transformation-Specific Smoothing (TPS), which combines two key techniques. First, TPS employs a weighted average of predictor predictions tailored to the transformation type, effectively filtering out adversarial inputs. Additionally, TPS incorporates a transformation-aware regularization term into the loss function, further enhancing point cloud model security. Through our testing, we found that TPS successfully mitigates adversarial attacks on the LeNet, ResNet, and MobileNet models, with negligible accuracy losses across various point cloud networks.

We're exploring the performance of two protocols - Slotted ALOHA and CSMA - for use in Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar networks operating at 24 GHz and analyzing how they adapt to avoid interference. Our radar system utilizes a sweep-and-wait approach, where each radar node continuously transmits data packets in a designated bandwidth while monitoring nearby radar activity to prevent collisions. As the radar nodes adjust to minimize interference, they update the transmission timing, creating a distributed database entry, known as the radar schedule, governing activity levels in the network. Through analytical and stochastic modeling, we investigate the average network throughput and collision rates for both Slotted ALOHA and CSMA protocols. Our results indicate that while CSMA outperforms Slotted ALOHA in radar networks by nearly doubling the maximum achievable throughput. Moreover, as the number of nodes in the radar network increases, the performance difference between CSMA and Slotted ALOHA protocols becomes more pronounced.

Recent experiments employing various methods have sought to detect the coupled absorption phenomenon when two photons interact with a material. To gain a deeper understanding, this study explores the implications of entangled two-photon absorption effects on HOM interference experiments through spectral analysis. By utilizing a mathematical framework, we demonstrate that a narrow-wavelength quantum dot can exhibit HOM interference even when subject to coupled absorption, provided that emitted photons maintain a defined frequency. Our analysis also indicates that a broad-spectrum quantum dot cannot display HOM interference despite being affected by coupled absorption, as it cannot maintain a consistent frequency. These findings offer valuable insight into identifying entangled two-photon absorption effects through HOM interference experiments.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05 and Beh17/Beh20, respectively, extends linearly from CP(1) to CP(V).

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Existing methods have focused primarily on modeling event representations
using recurrent neural networks and rank-based scoring functions, which are both
dependent on specific architectures. In contrast, our proposed method, LARK, uses
low-dimensional vectors to encode events and relies on a score function that is
not tied to a particular model. As a result, LARK is capable of leveraging the
information within entire temporal sequences and can even determine the most
appropriate time frame for an event by considering the temporal relationships with
related events. Due to its model-agnostic score function, LARK can also utilize
pre-trained knowledge that is embedded in word embeddings. Our experimental
results demonstrate that LARK surpasses state-of-the-art temporal knowledge graph
completers when evaluated using a dataset specifically tailored for event and
temporal information, while also producing more accurate results than the best
existing architecture-based approach on a complementary dataset.

In outdoor audio scenes, the ground sound holds significant importance as a clue for navigating through complex environments. Unfortunately, existing research on auditory navigation has largely overlooked its significance, focusing instead on audible cues like footsteps and rustling leaves. Our proposed approach aims to rectify this oversight by developing a novel method for ground sound extraction and a corresponding navigation paradigm that leverages learned sound source patterns. Through thorough testing, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of our extraction method and showcased its value in auditory navigation, both in isolation and in conjunction with existing auditory cues.

A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality known as Bellinequality-free approach actually relies on perfect correlations, which are uncommon in practical applications where imperfect correlations are more typical. However, we show that the Bellinequality-free approach can be effectively utilized with correlations of any strength, making it more versatile than previously thought. Moreover, our findings also highlight the potential of nonlocality in scenarios involving multiple parties.

In flat band systems, constrained environments result in atypical behaviors influenced by randomness, indicating minimal movement. Molecular orbital representations of these systems reveal the intricacies of this phenomenon. Mathematical arguments based on molecular modeling are employed to analyze the impact of chirality and symmetry on localization, demonstrating the distinct roles these features play.

A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm phase, exhibits an unconventional tendency towards superconductivity at low temperatures. Utilizing a computational approach that accounts for vibrational effects, our analysis reveals that superconductivity in this material is minimal, primarily occurring at very low temperatures and largely confined to certain H-$p_x$ and H-$p_y$ orbital combinations. Conversely, no superconducting phenomenon is observed within the H-$p_z$ orbital component. Upon further examination, it becomes evident that the commonly observed 2$\lambda$ superconducting pattern is replaced by a 1$\lambda$ pattern in this material. Ultimately, a maximal superconducting critical temperature of 13.5 K is achieved, significantly lower than previously estimated values.

Our primary goal is to examine a specific type of graph, G_f, that is derived from a division of a network, P, into separate areas or components, where each component, C_i, comprises a ring structure with 'i' nodes, connected in a circular pattern. We seek to determine the number of distinct ways to organize these separate components, where the edges within each ring can be utilized in varying capacities, in a topology isomorphic to P. We aim to identify a functional pattern, p(n,k), that represents the number of distinct topologies in a network with n nodes and k components, where each component is a ring of size k.

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their stable components, characteristics, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. To accomplish this, we study the movement patterns over the characteristics of the part of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, particularly demonstrating the rigidity where any stable movement remains unchanged, which is a more comprehensive interpretation of Furstenberg's earlier work concerning patterns on the torus.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To ensure reliability, developers employ advanced control techniques, including redundancy in sensors and computation processes, and contingency strategies, such as automatic emergency braking, to mitigate and respond to potential system failures. To further strengthen the system, we apply formal verification techniques to assess and validate the reliability of these contingency measures during failures. Specifically, our study utilizes the Isabelle/HOL proof assistant to formally verify the correct functioning of a sub-system responsible for detecting and responding to failures on the road.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, and language is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional distance-based clustering methods ineffective. In response, researchers have developed an alternative approach, Influence Based Clustering, which utilizes the inherent properties of these systems to group similar entities. Although initially designed for static systems, this method requires significant modifications when applied to dynamic systems. In an effort to enhance its accuracy and efficiency, an updated algorithm, DBIBC, is presented, capable of clustering dynamic systems by integrating temporal data into the clustering process. Moreover, an optimized version, FastDBIBC, is introduced, which significantly reduces computational complexity while maintaining performance. In addition to these updates, an extensive case study is provided, demonstrating the effectiveness of these methods on real-world network data.

Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has employed the concepts of cuts, limits, and germs to reconstruct its mathematical processes. This study builds upon those findings, comparing three distinct frameworks for understanding the procedures of Leibnizian calculus: the integral, the comparison, and the symbolic frameworks. The investigation demonstrates that the frameworks are not only compatible with one another but also offer unique insights into the core methods of Leibnizian calculus. A significant outcome of this analysis is that the integral framework provides a more accurate representation of Leibnizian infinitesimal procedures than previously acknowledged in the literature.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using data from interferometric HI intensity mapping surveys. We simulate a realisation of these predictions using the FFTLog technique and release the tables publicly. By examining the effects of foreground removal on the HI power spectrum, we find that using a quadratic estimate significantly reduces bias at the expense of increasing noise. This impact becomes more substantial at higher redshifts where the signal is weaker and contaminated by more foregrounds. We find that at $z=2$, the bias is reduced but noise is increased, compared to $z=0.5$. We also find that using a quadratic estimate raises the estimate of $\Omega_m$ by approximately $0.05$, while using a linear estimate gives a lower estimate of $\Omega_m$ with differences less than $0.01$. We find that to accurately recover the mean HI density we require a low noise level, and that using a quadratic estimate with low noise allows for recovery with minimal impact from foregrounds on spatially varying coefficients. This estimate gives a recovered value within $0.1\sigma$ of the true value, whereas with noise dominated spectra the estimate is $5\sigma$ from the true value.

This paper explores the connection between independence of quantum operators and their dimension in quantum systems. We establish that infinite dimension is a necessary condition for operator independence. By constructing specific models, we demonstrate that operator independence does not necessarily imply a lower dimension than the total Hilbert space, and further, that it can coexist with a countably infinite dimension. However, we prove that in the absence of superselection sectors, operator independence implies a lower dimension equal to the total Hilbert space dimension. Our work also considers the implications for basic commutation relations and predicted no-go theorems for infinite-dimensional systems with independent operators.

Recommender systems are increasingly popular solutions for addressing information overload and discovering relevant items. Given the distinct strengths of context-based and collaborative filtering approaches, integrating them into hybrid methods yields improved accuracy and scalability. This research aims to enhance a hybrid recommender system by combining three components: (1) a document-based method for modeling semantic relationships between items and users, (2) a collaborative filtering method for leveraging user-item interaction data, and (3) a user-based similarity measure for aggregating and balancing the contributions of each approach. By effectively balancing the influence of each method, this hybrid architecture achieves better performance than its individual counterparts and static hybrids.

Independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) matrix entries from the real or complex unit sphere lead to Wigner matrices with simple spectrum that converges asymptotically. Building upon this, more complex structure can be accounted for by adding off-diagonal or rank-one perturbations to Wigner matrices, denoted as type-A or rank-one perturbations, characterized by non-zero trace. A fourth category, type-B, refers to combinations of these modifications, featuring non-zero trace but negligible diagonal elements. As the size of these matrices increases indefinitely, statistical characteristics, such as the linear spectral distribution, emerge and become stable. Type-B matrices exhibit unique properties, such as frequency-wise almost sure spectral bulk convergence and unique asymptotic almost linear spectral statistics. Furthermore, the eigenvalues of these matrices behave independently and, upon meeting the necessary conditions, certain matrix subsets are free in the classical probability theory sense.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in two scenarios. In the first case, where the future is constant, we demonstrate how to adapt existing monitoring approaches for constant futures to accommodate changing timelines. In the second case, involving shifting futures, we introduce a new monitoring approach based on a well-known and established algorithm. Additionally, this paper provides monitoring software, called Chronometer, which facilitates the monitoring of Timed B\"uchi Automata. We also present a case study illustrating the practical applications of monitoring during a field trial in healthcare.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. Attention is focused on isospin breaking and
the mixing between $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$, both of which are generated by meson-meson interactions. By using isospin breaking and the calculated $f_0(980)-a_0(980)$ mixing, a numerical prediction for the branching ratio ${\cal B}(\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980))$ is made.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical capabilities: a pupil tracker, a pupil sampler, a pupil rotator, and a pupil imaging camera, which combine to facilitate efficient characterization of the GRAVITY laboratory's pupil intensity distribution. Through systemic calculations and carefully controlled physical measurements, the optical setup's accuracy and error margins were determined. Consequently, a reliable method for thoroughly examining and understanding the optical properties of GRAVITY's laboratory was established. This resulted in an in-depth characterization of the optical characteristics of the telescope's light entering the instrument, allowing for optimal configuration of the device and maximal observation accuracy.

We introduce a expanded version of the k-Center problem, which requires us to identify the smallest set of r centers capable of reducing overall cost. This modified problem, generalized k-Center, necessitates that any two points within a given point set be connected by a sequence of at most s intermediary points. Our goal is to minimize the size of the supporting set. This problem can be related to graphs with a limited doubling structure or highway dimension, yet we show they are not equivalent using our proposed characterization. Specifically, we provide an example of a metric space with a limited highway dimension but doubling dimension of n, and prove that finding an optimal solution for generalized k-Center on such space is an NP-hard problem, even with the centers restricted to a fixed set. This result also implies the same intractability for other related problems, including the generalized k-Traveling Salesman problem.

In our paper, it are solved and mirrored the questions regarding the distinction between identical and uniquely valued functions within specific categories, such as entire functions and their shifted differences, under the constraints of specific differential equations.

This study explores solving polynomial linear systems in the case of errors, and we develop a solver based on the Chinese Remainder Theorem that works with a specific type of error. We present new estimates for the parameters that govern when and how this solver terminates. To illustrate the performance improvements offered by our solutions, we created a benchmark that showcases the impact of our innovations. Specifically, in systems with a large number of equations and unknowns, and in the presence of errors, our solver exhibits improved behavior.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we identify a new type of photon bundle emission protected by parity. This parity-symmetry-protected bundle emission occurs in a scenario where both the cavity and the two-level emitter possess spin, but only when all three quantities have odd values. Furthermore, the emitter must be positioned at a position with parity-dependent characteristics to give rise to this protected bundle emission effect. It is noteworthy that, in the absence of this parity constraint, the emitter's spin would lead to the destruction of the bundle emission via emission of double-photon states. This parity-symmetry-protected bundle emission offers a distinct signature for distinguishing between odd- and even-spin emitters in experiments.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored. By utilizing a finite lowest-order local effective Lagrangian derived from QED for ρ and ω mesons, a mixed action approach is employed, where the Lagrangian is coupled to both bosonic and fermionic fields. A local medium with chiral imbalance, facilitated through the vacuum of fermions, is considered, with specific attention to the case of one flavor. Notably, both vacuum polarization and self-energy induced by fermions are found to contribute to the vector-meson spectral function. By summing relevant diagrams at finite temperature and chemical potential, a spectral function for the vector mesons is obtained, which is then used to determine the in-medium propagator and mass spectrum.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse graph's node count in a distributed setting, where the network is modeled as a small-world graph and each node initiates a distributed algorithm without prior knowledge of the graph's structure. To achieve this goal, we develop a distributed algorithm that estimates the graph's node count with a limited number of communication rounds and accurate margin of error, even when up to f faults occur. The algorithm's error rate and communication complexity are directly influenced by the failure threshold f and the minimum degree of the graph D. Specifically, for a graph with degree at least D and f <= D, the algorithm estimates the node count within a fraction of D over N, where N is the node count, using O(f^2) operations per node, and completing in at most O(f) rounds. When considering the extreme case where f approaches D, the algorithm still provides an estimate with a margin of error represented by a fraction of D over N, using the same number of operations and rounds.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, a challenge arises in linking continuous initial conditions to discrete grid points, especially when attempting to enforce constraints. Our group has developed a novel method, CTTK, to streamline this process, allowing for the emergence of arbitrary frequency components in the initial displacement of the matter, while maintaining stability. Unlike fixed gauge conditions, CTTK doesn't introduce an additional lapse term that can disrupt the solution, and it doesn't restrict the frequency spectrum of the displacement. By contrast, CTTK preserves the Poisson equation for the metric, simplifying the solution process and making it possible to calculate the metric without additional constraints.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves identifying the neutrino mass ordering by using a large, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector equipped with photomultiplier tubes. Accurate energy reconstruction and event categorization heavily rely on the precise reconstruction of event images through the PMTs. Consequently, the selection of high-quality PMTs with optimal characteristics is crucial for the experiment. Before making the final selection, the experiment undertook a comprehensive testing program of the 20-inch PMTs, which included testing the absolute photometric accuracy, spatial homogeneity, and polarization of the PMTs at the Jiangmen University of Science and Technology's laboratory. Data analysis and qualification procedures for these tests are presented in this document.

Developing accurate forecasts for complex multidimensional time series data remains challenging due to its inherent nonlinear characteristics and unpredictability. Despite advancements in models like ARIMA, LSTM, GRU, and GRU-AR, they often struggle with feature selection, model generalizability, and computational efficiency. To address these limitations, this paper presents a novel adaptive graph convolutional network framework, AGCF, which leverages an adaptive filter to effectively capture both short-term and long-term patterns in multidimensional time series data. The proposed framework's performance is demonstrated through extensive evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets of various dimensions, resulting in significant improvements over existing models.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, are particularly prone to this distortion. Previous studies have developed atmospheric models to accurately predict atmospheric dispersion, but a comprehensive analysis of these models has yet to be conducted.
